players.product: electrical and mechanical construction and installation of data-center power and cooling systems

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center scope and reach (CEO Tony Guzzi; his turns are labelled 'Moderator' in the saved transcript): the predominance of EMCOR's data-center business is still cloud infrastructure, 'growing 9% a year', with builds 'somewhere between 20 and 50, 75 megawatts', while EMCOR participates in the shift to much larger AI sites. On a 200-megawatt data center EMCOR does 'probably 1.5 to 2 times' the mechanical scope of a cloud data center ('It is the heat') and electrically 'that might be 1.25 to 1.5'. He no longer counts data-center markets one by one (formerly 'seven markets now mechanically and 16 electrically'): 'Electrically, we're probably servicing 50% of the markets that matter, 60%. Mechanically, somewhere around 40%, 50%, a little less', with fire protection everywhere in the country. 'For the most part, our customers aren't people like Anthropic and OpenAI.'
quarterly_data.figure: AI data center vs cloud scope: mechanical 1.5 to 2 times, electrical 1.25 to 1.5; about 50%-60% of key markets electrically, about 40%-50% mechanically

quarterly_data.signal: Acquisitions (Guzzi): EMCOR announced 5 electrical deals with '$600 million in revenue trailing, $100 million, give or take, of EBITDA', the two biggest being Schmidt (Central Texas) and Connelly (outside Chicago); both closed in early August (CFO Jason Nalbandian: 'Early August'). Their growth is expected to come mainly from more data-center exposure, teaming with existing EMCOR companies - Gibson & Lyons-Pinner in Chicago, and in Central Texas Morley-Moss, bought in 2018 and 'now 10 times the size it was'. EMCOR does over $1 billion of revenue in Texas outside the oil and gas business, without Schmidt. Purchase prices not stated.
quarterly_data.figure: 5 electrical acquisitions: about $600 million trailing revenue and about $100 million EBITDA; Schmidt and Connelly closed early August

quarterly_data.signal: Growth mix (CFO Jason Nalbandian): first-half 2026 organic growth was about 18.3%; stripping out high-tech manufacturing (semiconductors, biotech) and network and communications (data centers), EMCOR still grew organically around 9%, with building services up about 5% organically and EMCOR Industrial Services up 15% organically. High-tech manufacturing is roughly 40% semiconductors, 40% biotech and 20% EV battery work, now at a base 'almost 1.5 times what it was in 2023' (a three-year CAGR of almost 11%); 'some of the growth we've seen recently in data centers did come at the expense of semiconductors'. Guzzi: of about six geographic semiconductor markets that matter EMCOR is in four, and in one state it will 'sit out the next round of the fab' because a bigger data-center build is under way there; a chunk of pharma work is tied to GLP-1s.
quarterly_data.figure: first-half 2026 organic growth about 18.3% (about 9% excluding high-tech and data centers); high-tech about 1.5 times the 2023 base, almost 11% three-year CAGR

quarterly_data.signal: Capex and margin bands (CFO): over a five-year period revenue CAGR is about 14%, 15% while capex CAGR is about 28% to 30%, the difference being investment in prefabrication shops (new fabrication space, expansions, automation); capex is 0.6% to 0.65% of revenues 'and I think that holds into 2027 and 2028'. Guzzi: about 20%-25% of capex is maintenance and absolute capex dollars do not step down. Sustainable margins on a rolling 12- to 24-month view: consolidated operating margin around the 9.5%-9.8% guidance; electrical between 12% and 13%, mechanical between 12% and 12.5%, building services 6% to 6.5%, industrial right around 3%.
quarterly_data.figure: capex 0.6% to 0.65% of revenue into 2027 and 2028; segment margin bands electrical 12%-13%, mechanical 12%-12.5%, building services 6%-6.5%, industrial about 3%

quarterly_data.signal: Contracting and constraints (Guzzi): EMCOR is 'still predominantly a fixed-price contractor' but the more complex, larger AI data-center designs push work - especially mechanical, where cooling and piping designs may change mid-job - toward guaranteed-maximum-price terms; 'We have one client that that is how they build', and on the largest job the customer sometimes helps pay part of EMCOR's fabrication cost to expand an on-site facility, with generous general conditions to attract labour. The critical bottleneck to growth is supervision (foremen, superintendents, project managers), not tradespeople. For the next 3 years customers 'pretty much know what they're going to build'; he says the gas turbines needed for data-center power were sold off through 2031 and power is 'the real question'.
